properties.title: Toward Verifiable Medical Imaging World Models: An Engineering Framework for Evaluating Simulation Fidelity, Roll-Out Stability, and Clinical Plausibility
Toward Verifiable Medical Imaging World Models: An Engineering Framework for Evaluating Simulation Fidelity, Roll-Out Stability, and Clinical Plausibility

properties.name: Three verification axes and four fidelity layers
properties.content: Simulation fidelity, free-running rollout stability and clinical plausibility/reliability precede clinical-benefit claims. Fidelity layers distinguish signal, anatomy, physiology and causality; individual alternative-treatment outcomes remain unobserved.
properties.attribution: This paper own taxonomy/recommendation; not an implemented cited system

properties.name: First-crossing horizon contract
properties.content: For observed-policy trajectories, effective horizon is the longest prefix whose horizon-specific chosen loss quantile remains within an explicit clinical tolerance. Patient-cluster bootstrap, uncertainty intervals and strata are proposed. Passing at a later time does not undo an earlier failure.
properties.attribution: This paper own taxonomy/recommendation; not an implemented cited system

properties.name: Worked example limitation
properties.content: Approximate digitized EHRWorld chloride relative errors with illustrative tolerance0.12 give4versus2rounds. Source aggregate curves are not patient-level quantiles, the tolerance is illustrative and the example does not validate off-policy planning support.
properties.attribution: This paper own taxonomy/recommendation; not an implemented cited system

properties.name: Claim-proportionate reporting contract
properties.content: Eight reporting items accumulate across passive prediction, action-conditioned prediction, counterfactual comparison and planning tiers. Nine-model purposive audit measures reported evidence, not an exhaustive frequency estimate or confirmed absence of system capability.
properties.attribution: This paper own taxonomy/recommendation; not an implemented cited system

Consistent with the diagnostic aim of the paper, the sam-
ple was selected to represent the imaging capability ladder
and both imaging families rather than to provide exhaustive
coverage. The resulting audit should therefore be interpreted
as a characterization of current reporting practices within a
curated set of representative models, rather than as a preva-
lence estimate for the literature as a whole.
Veriﬁcation vs. Validation: An Engineering
Framing
The word trust conceals two questions that the medical world
model literature often runs together: veriﬁcation and valida-
tion. V eriﬁcation asks whether a system behaves according
to its speciﬁcation. V alidation asks whether the system meets
the real-world need for which it was developed.
For a medical world model, validation asks whether using
the model improves patient outcomes, clinical decisions, or
efﬁciency. This is an empirical and often prospective ques-
tion. V eriﬁcation asks a prior question that can largely be
addressed during model development: given that the model
generates simulated trajectories, are those trajectories cor-
rect at the claimed level of description, stable under roll-out,
and behaviorally sensible under the interventions the model
represents? A model may satisfy these veriﬁcation require-
ments and still fail to provide clinical beneﬁt, but without
such evidence there is little basis for trusting the simulated
trajectories on which later clinical claims depend.

ASME V&V 40 provides a risk-informed framework for
assessing the credibility of computational models in medical-
device applications, based on the model’s context of use, its
inﬂuence on a decision, and the consequences of an incorrect
decision [ 18]. Our claim-proportionate framework follows
the same general principle, but applies it speciﬁcally to
learned medical imaging world models. The terminology also
differs. In V&V 40, veriﬁcation concerns whether the compu-
tational model is implemented and solved correctly, whereas
comparison of model predictions with real-world data falls
under validation. In this paper, we use veriﬁcation more
broadly for the developer-side evidence needed to assess sim-
ulated trajectories before claims of clinical beneﬁt are made.
The contribution here is therefore not the principle of propor-
tionate evidence itself, but its operationalization for learned
roll-out models through layered simulation ﬁdelity, multi-
step stability, the effective planning horizon, and explicit
treatment of counterfactual limitations.
Axis 1—Simulation Fidelity
The ﬁrst and most basic veriﬁcation question is whether the
states a model predicts are correct. This is the axis on which
current practice reports most heavily, yet it is also the one
where reported numbers most often measure the wrong thing.
The difﬁculty is not that ﬁdelity metrics are absent, but that
ﬁdelity is treated as a single quantity when it is in fact layered,
and the layer a metric captures is frequently not the layer at
which the model operates or makes its claim.
Fidelity Is Layered
We ﬁnd it useful to distinguish four layers at which a pre-
dicted medical state can be judged correct, ordered from the
most superﬁcial to the most demanding.
The ﬁrst is signal or perceptual ﬁdelity: whether

Over a short horizon the effect is often invisible, which is
precisely why single-step metrics look reassuring. Over the
longer horizons that make a world model useful for plan-
ning, small per-step errors accumulate into trajectories that
depart from anything physiologically or anatomically real.
The problem is compounded for action-conditioned models,
because two sources of error accumulate together: error in
estimating the evolving state, and error in modeling how the
state responds to each action. A model may be individually
competent at both and still produce untrustworthy long-
horizon roll-outs once the two interact across many steps.
This is not a hypothetical concern imported from other
ﬁelds, though the broader world-model literature recognizes
it explicitly. Work on video world models as simulators notes
that long-horizon roll-outs are prone to hallucination, with
global scene structure drifting and backgrounds collapsing
as roll-out length grows, and treats roll-out stability as a
ﬁrst-class design target rather than an afterthought [ 19]. The
medical literature contains the same phenomenon, often vis-
ible in the very papers that set out to ﬁx it. EHRWorld [ 14]
reports the trajectory of relative error across successive sim-
ulation rounds and motivates its causally grounded training
precisely by the need to reduce error accumulation and to
remain stable during clinically sensitive events, an implicit
acknowledgment that naive simulators do neither. med-
Dreamer [ 15], which relies on latent imagination to train
a treatment policy, depends for its validity on imagined tra-
jectories that remain close enough to real physiology to be
safe substitutes for it, which is a roll-out stability requirement
even when it is not named as such.
The Effective Planning Horizon
These observations motivate a summary quantity that we
believe medical world models should be expected to report,
and which almost none currently do. Informally, the effective
planning horizon is the span over which a model’s roll-
outs stay trustworthy. We now make that statement precise,
because a measure this central should be deﬁned rather than
gestured at.

reference trajectory is unobserved. Heff should therefore
not be interpreted as an off-policy or counterfactual plan-

should be reported together with the action distribution used

A model that compares treatments through imagined
trajectories should therefore report whether its effective
planning horizon reaches the horizon over which those tra-
jectories are compared.
Computing the Effective Planning Horizon
The deﬁnition in “The Effective Planning Horizon” translates
directly into an estimation procedure, given in Algorithm 1,
that a developer can run on retrospective roll-outs. The pro-
cedure rolls each held-out initial state forward to a horizon
cap, scores every step with a modality-appropriate loss, sum-
marizes the per-horizon loss by the chosen quantile to form
the degradation curve, and reads off the horizon at the curve’s
ﬁrst crossing of the clinical tolerance. A trajectory boot-
strap supplies an uncertainty interval, and the same routine
restricted to a subgroup yields the stratiﬁed horizons of “Axis
3—Clinical Plausibility and Reliability .” The ﬁrst-crossing
rule encodes the convention that recovery after a breach earns
no credit.
As a worked illustration of the ﬁrst-crossing calcula-
tion, we digitized the horizon-resolved chloride relative-error
curves reported for EHRWorld and GPT-5.2 in Figure 1 of
EHRWorld [14]. The values are approximate because they
were digitized from the published ﬁgure rather than provided
numerically. Using an illustrative tolerance of τ = 0.12, the
EHRWorld curve remains within tolerance through round 4
and ﬁrst exceeds it at round 5, giving an illustrativeHeff = 4.
The GPT-5.2 curve ﬁrst exceeds the same tolerance at round
3, giving Heff = 2 (Fig. 1). This calculation illustrates the
ﬁrst-crossing rule only: EHRWorld does not report these
curves as quantiles over trajectories, so they should not be
interpreted as empirical estimates of Heff(τ, q) under the full
deﬁnition in Eq. 2.

conditioned, and reporting both the degradation curve and
Heff at a stated tolerance (Items 3 and 4, “ A Minimal
Reporting Standard for Medical World Models ”). In the

whether that correctness survives roll-out. The third axis con-
cerns whether simulations that are internally sound are also
adequate to inform action: whether the model’s responses
to interventions are sensible, whether its conﬁdence bears
a defensible relation to its accuracy, and whether its com-
petence holds across the patients who will encounter it. We
name this axis clinical plausibility and reliability rather than
clinical validity, deliberately, because the latter term invites
confusion with clinical validation, and because the properties
grouped here differ sharply in how far they can be established
at all from the retrospective evidence a developer holds.
The properties a medical world model would ideally pos-
sess along this axis fall into three epistemic categories, and
conﬂating them is the source of much of the over-claiming
the ﬁeld is prone to.
The ﬁrst category is testable properties: those that can
be checked directly against held-out data and yield a mea-
sured value or a pass. Calibration and subgroup performance
belong here. They are directly testable using held-out data,
and their absence from a paper is a reporting gap rather than
a fundamental limit.
The second is falsiﬁable-only consistency conditions:
checks that cannot conﬁrm a prediction is correct but can
catch predictions that are obviously wrong. The counterfactual-
consistency checks below belong here. Passing them estab-
lishes that a model’s intervention responses are not incoher-
ent with known clinical structure. It does not establish that
they are right. Their value is real but strictly negative; they
can falsify but not conﬁrm.
The third is unidentiﬁed claims: those that cannot be
established from observational data even in principle. True
counterfactual correctness, and the causal or mechanistic
ﬁdelity discussed in “ Axis 1—Simulation Fidelity ,” belong

Method
We audit the nine imaging world models identiﬁed in “Model
Selection,” four in longitudinal radiological imaging and
disease progression and ﬁve in surgical and endoscopic
video, spanning the imaging capability ladder from pas-
sive temporal prediction through counterfactual roll-out. For
each model we recorded nine attributes (Table 1): modal-
ity; highest claimed capability tier; the highest ﬁdelity layer
implicated by the claim and the highest layer at which evi-
dence is reported (“ Axis 1—Simulation Fidelity ”); whether
multi-step evaluation is reported and whether it is resolved
across the horizon (Section “ Axis 2—Roll-Out Stability ”);
and whether the paper reports a counterfactual-consistency
check, uncertainty estimates, and a subgroup breakdown
(“Axis 3—Clinical Plausibility and Reliability ”). Scoring
reﬂects what each primary source reports; an absence records
that a capability is unveriﬁed on the published record, not that
the model lacks it.
The Audit Matrix
The complete scoring is given in Table 1, using the ﬁdelity-
layer (S, A, P , C) and capability-tier (T1–T4) codes deﬁned
in its caption. “Y es” indicates that the evidence is reported in
the primary source, “–” that it is not reported, “Part.” that it is
partial, “Impl.” that it is implicit (treatment-conditioned but
not tested for coherence), and “n/a” that the category does not
apply to the model’s design. Absence of reported evidence is
an observation about the published record, not a claim that
the model lacks the underlying capability.
What the Audit Shows
Four patterns emerge, each traceable to the reported evidence
in Table 1.
The ﬁrst is a systematic gap between the ﬁdelity layer a
model claims and the layer at which it reports evidence, most
pronounced in surgical video. Models whose stated purpose
implicates the physiological or causal layers are frequently
evidenced most strongly at the signal or structural layers.
SurgWorld (Cosmos-H-Surgical) [20] and the Suturing world
model [ 22] are representative: both target physically plau-
sible, action-relevant surgical dynamics, yet report ﬁdelity
chieﬂy through video quality and L2 reconstruction respec-
tively, which are signal-layer quantities. SurgVeo [10] is the
exception, being the model that most directly probes the
physiological and procedural layers, and doing so only by
abandoning automated metrics for structured expert assess-
ment, which is precisely how it exposes the shortfall of
the signal-layer metrics its peers rely upon. TaDiff [ 6], the
anatomy-focused CheXWorld [7] and Xray2Xray [8], and the
physiology-focused SurgVista [21] come closest to matching
evidence to claim, and they do so by evaluating at the layer
they target rather than defaulting to perceptual scores.
The second pattern is more encouraging than an earlier
reading of the ﬁeld would suggest, and it concerns roll-out
stability. A ﬁrst wave of imaging world models evaluated

Item 0 (capability claim) is a declaration that determines which rows
apply and is therefore not scored here. Items 1–2 (simulation ﬁdelity)
apply to every model, Items 3–4 (roll-out stability), 6 (calibration), and 7
(subgroup) switch on once a model conditions on actions, Item 5 (coun-
terfactual consistency) applies from the counterfactual tier upward, and
Item 8 (explicit veriﬁcation/validation status) is required of planning-
tier models, which make the strongest clinical claims
not. A useful next step would be to apply the framework in full
to a small number of existing models and test whether per-
formance across the three axes predicts behavior on held-out
or prospective trajectories. Completing the reporting items
therefore documents the available evidence; it does not by
itself demonstrate adequate veriﬁcation or clinical beneﬁt.
The effective planning horizon depends on a ﬁdelity loss
and a clinical tolerance that we deliberately leave open
because appropriate choices differ across modalities and clin-
ical timescales. Horizons computed using different losses or
tolerances are therefore not directly comparable. Reporting
Heff(τ) across a range of tolerances partly addresses this,
but modality-speciﬁc losses, clinically agreed tolerances, and
shared benchmarks remain to be developed. In addition, Heff
is estimated under the observed action policy and does not
establish reliability under the alternative actions required for
counterfactual comparison or planning.
The audit covers nine purposively selected imaging world
models and should not be interpreted as a prevalence esti-
mate for the wider ﬁeld. It records what each paper reports,
not what the underlying model may be capable of. A
future extension should use a systematic search, independent
double-coding, and direct re-evaluation of selected models
under a common protocol.
Finally, the reporting standard is provisional. Its items
should be reﬁned through use and clinical consensus, and its
most natural role may be as a world-model-speciﬁc extension
of existing reporting guidance such as TRIPOD+AI rather
than as a standalone certiﬁcation instrument.
Conclusion
Medical world models are designed to simulate how a
patient’s state may evolve under interventions and, in more
ambitious systems, to compare or plan from imagined tra-
jectories. Their value therefore depends on whether these
roll-outs remain faithful and stable. We frame their evalua-
tion around three axes: simulation ﬁdelity, roll-out stability,
and clinical plausibility and reliability, while separating this
developer-side evidence from later clinical validation.
